spring.title: Spring at Kingfisher Hollow
spring.intro: Spring begins with rain and thaw in the low places. Woodland flowers make the most of the light before the trees leaf out, and frogs and insects become part of life around the warming water.
spring.next_observation: How long does spring light reach the forest floor? Return to a patch of trout lily as the trees leaf out and see which flowers open as shade deepens.

passages.title: After the rain
passages.body: Rain and thaw fill shallow pools in the woods. In New York, spotted salamanders leave their winter shelters on mild, rainy nights and move to these pools to lay eggs.
passages.look_for: From a dry bank, look for clusters of dark salamander eggs suspended in clear or milky jelly just below the surface.

claims.text: Spotted salamander eggs mark that early-spring transition at the Hollow.

passages.title: Under the open canopy
passages.body: Spring wildflowers brighten the forest floor while the branches are still bare. Trout lilies make use of that brief window of sunlight, followed in May by white starflower blooms as shade deepens.
passages.look_for: Look for mottled trout lily leaves low in the litter, then for the white points of starflower held above a ring of leaves in May.

passages.title: Life at the water's edge
passages.body: By late spring, the canopy shades the woodland floor while the pond still catches the sun. Gray treefrogs can call from branches near breeding water, and adult dragonflies hunt along sunny water margins.
passages.look_for: Listen for a gray treefrog’s short trill from branches near water. At the pond margin, watch for a baskettail making repeated passes low over the water.

rows.name: Spotted Salamander
rows.interpretation: Spotted salamanders lay their eggs in jelly-covered masses in spring pools. Green algae can grow inside the masses and supply oxygen as the embryos develop.

sources.label: Experimental study of algae in spotted salamander eggs

rows.name: Clemens’ Agonopterix
rows.interpretation: Clemens’ Agonopterix survives winter as an adult and can fly again when the weather warms. Its caterpillars feed inside folded leaves of carrot-family plants.

sources.label: North Carolina State Parks account of Clemens’ Agonopterix
Tompkins County study of Clemens’ Agonopterix host plants

rows.name: yellow trout lily
rows.interpretation: Yellow trout lilies use the short stretch of sunlight between snowmelt and canopy closure. After the flowers set seed, ants carry the seeds away for the rich morsel attached to each one.

sources.label: Research on the trout lily’s spring light window
Duke Gardens on trout lily and seed dispersal by ants

rows.name: northern starflower
rows.interpretation: In late spring, northern starflower lifts white blooms above a ring of leaves. The plant also spreads below ground, where tubers send up new shoots.

sources.label: Kasey Hartz Natural Area account of northern starflower

rows.name: Gray Treefrog
rows.interpretation: From late spring, male gray treefrogs trill from shrubs and branches near breeding water. Broad toe pads help them grip the stems and branches they climb.

sources.label: Maryland DNR on gray treefrog calls and habitat

rows.name: Common Baskettail
rows.interpretation: Common Baskettails patrol pond margins in late spring and early summer. A female carries a cluster of eggs at the tip of her abdomen and deposits it among floating plants or algae.

sources.label: University of Nebraska State Museum on baskettail patrols and season
Wisconsin Odonata Survey on Common Baskettail egg laying
New York State DEC on spring amphibian movements
Trout lily and the northern hardwood spring light window
University of Maine on starflower
Maryland DNR on Gray Treefrog habitat and seasonal calls

bird_examples.name: Rusty Blackbird
bird_examples.note: This April checklist records Rusty Blackbird at Kingfisher Hollow on one visit.

summer.title: Summer at Kingfisher Hollow
summer.intro: Summer settles in around the pond and creek. Dragonflies hunt above the water by day, moths fly after dusk, and plants fill in the wet margins as the season advances.
summer.next_observation: Do pondhawks return to the same perch after a short flight? Watch a sunny stretch of bank and see which low stems they come back to.

passages.title: The pond in daylight
passages.body: A dragonfly's life straddles the waterline. A mature nymph climbs out of the water and sheds its skin, then takes to the air to hunt once its wings harden.
passages.look_for: Check stems rising from the pond for the empty skins dragonflies leave behind. Watch for an adult pondhawk making short flights from a low perch.

claims.text: Eastern Pondhawks are among the dragonflies of midsummer at the Hollow.

passages.title: After dark
passages.body: Warm summer evenings extend insect activity beyond daylight. As dragonflies settle for the night, many moths take to the air around the woods and field edges.
passages.look_for: As dusk deepens on a warm evening, notice which moths settle nearby. A Lettered Habrosyne has pale zigzag bands across its wings.

claims.text: The Lettered Habrosyne is among the moths active after dusk at the Hollow.

passages.title: The tangle at the creek edge
passages.body: By late summer, plants fill in the wet margins of the creek. Arrow-leaved tearthumb threads its stems through streamside growth, and vegetation in shallow water can offer cover for crayfish.
passages.look_for: Look for arrow-shaped tearthumb leaves where prickly stems weave through the bankside plants. In the shallows, look for crayfish moving between patches of cover.

rows.name: Eastern Pondhawk
rows.interpretation: Eastern Pondhawks hunt around ponds and other slow water in summer. They launch from low perches and can catch flying insects nearly their own size.

sources.label: Wisconsin Odonata Survey on Eastern Pondhawk
North Carolina State Parks dragonfly accounts

rows.name: Pickerel Frog
rows.interpretation: Pickerel frogs favor cool, wooded streams in summer and also leave the water to feed in nearby grassy openings.

sources.label: Minnesota DNR on Pickerel Frog summer habitat

rows.name: Lettered Habrosyne Moth
rows.interpretation: Adult Lettered Habrosynes fly after dusk in summer. Their caterpillars eat blackberry leaves, so the brambles at a woodland edge can support another stage of the same moth.

sources.label: North Carolina State Parks on Lettered Habrosyne host plants
Summer night encounter at Kingfisher Hollow

rows.name: arrow-leaved tearthumb
rows.interpretation: Arrow-leaved tearthumb scrambles over neighboring stems in wet places, helped by tiny backward-pointing prickles. Clusters of pale flowers open from midsummer into early autumn.

sources.label: University of Michigan on how arrow-leaved tearthumb climbs
Michigan State University on tearthumb flowering

rows.name: Calico Crayfish
rows.interpretation: Calico crayfish use underwater vegetation for cover in slow water. As water recedes, they can retreat into burrows.

sources.label: Michigan DNR field guide to crayfish
National Park Service on the dragonfly life cycle
University of Michigan on arrow-leaved tearthumb
Michigan DNR guide to crayfish and their habitats
National Park Service moth surveys at Acadia

autumn.title: Autumn at Kingfisher Hollow
autumn.intro: Goldenrods flower as the woods begin to change color. With leaf fall, fresh litter joins the wood already breaking down on the forest floor, and some insects stay active into November.
autumn.next_observation: Which insects are still active after leaf fall? On a sunny afternoon, watch for meadowhawks where bare ground catches the light. After dusk, look for moths on a mild evening.

passages.title: At the goldenrod edge
passages.body: Goldenrods flower along open edges while much of the canopy is still green. Their clusters of small yellow blooms supply pollen and nectar to insects into early autumn.
passages.look_for: Watch a goldenrod spray for bees and other insects visiting its small yellow blooms. Later in autumn, look for dry seed heads in the same patch.

claims.text: At the Hollow, flowering goldenrod is a recurring sign of September.

passages.title: Look down to fallen wood
passages.body: As leaves fall, they add a fresh layer of litter over branches and logs already breaking down. Fungi help return nutrients from dead wood to the forest floor. Puffballs and bracket fungi are among the forms that fruit on wood.
passages.look_for: Look along fallen wood for rounded clusters of puffballs and for shelves with gill-like ridges underneath.

passages.title: Along the bank and after dark
passages.body: As autumn cools, mild days and evenings can still bring insect activity. Dragonflies and moths can both extend the season after many of the leaves are down.
passages.look_for: On a cool, sunny day, watch for a meadowhawk basking on bare ground or wood. On a mild evening, notice whether moths such as the Bicolored Sallow are still flying.

claims.text: At the Hollow, both Bicolored Sallows and Autumn Meadowhawks can still turn up in November.

rows.name: wrinkle-leaved goldenrod
rows.interpretation: Wrinkle-leaved goldenrod opens sprays of small yellow flowers as summer turns to autumn. Bees and other insects feed on the nectar and pollen, and birds can eat the seeds that follow.

sources.label: USDA plant guide to wrinkle-leaved goldenrod

rows.name: Pear-shaped Puffball
rows.interpretation: Pear-shaped puffballs fruit in clusters on decaying logs and stumps in autumn. A pore opens at the top as each puffball ripens, releasing a cloud of spores when raindrops strike it.

sources.label: Ohio DNR field guide to stump puffballs

rows.name: Conifer Mazegill
rows.interpretation: Conifer Mazegill breaks down dead wood, especially conifers, leaving a brown rot. Its tough shelves can persist after leaf fall, with gill-like folds beneath.

sources.label: NC State Mycological Herbarium on Conifer Mazegill
Natural Resources Canada on Conifer Mazegill and brown rot

rows.name: Autumn Meadowhawk
rows.interpretation: Autumn Meadowhawks can bask on bare ground on cool days, then dart after small flying insects. Sun-warmed perches help them stay active well into autumn.

sources.label: Illinois DNR on Autumn Meadowhawk behavior
University of Wisconsin–Milwaukee Field Station on late flight

rows.name: Bicolored Sallow
rows.interpretation: Bicolored Sallows fly well into autumn. In spring, their young caterpillars can feed on opening red maple buds.

sources.label: North Carolina State Parks account of Bicolored Sallow
Bucknell University on goldenrod and its insects
US Forest Service on wood decay and forest fungi
New York State DEC on regional dragonfly seasons

winter.title: Winter at Kingfisher Hollow
winter.intro: Leaf fall opens the woods between the pond and creek. Some insects spend the cold months in shelter, while mammals that remain active leave tracks across the snow.
winter.next_observation: How does a track trail change over open ground, roots, and fallen wood? Follow a line of prints from the side and see where pairs draw together or spread apart.

passages.title: Read the open woods
passages.body: When hardwoods lose their leaves, more light reaches the ground and the conifers stay green. Snow and ice can accent the difference between the broad surface of the pond and the creek winding past it.
passages.look_for: From a safe bank, notice where snow gathers on still ice and where the creek’s current can keep a channel open.

passages.title: Check the sheltered edges
passages.body: Protected places carry some insects through winter. Adults of some species spend the cold months beneath loose bark or in sheltered cracks, ready to resume activity when conditions warm.
passages.look_for: On a mild day, check sheltered surfaces for a seed bug with a zigzag across its folded wings and flared hind legs. Leave bark and leaf litter in place.

claims.text: The Western Conifer Seed Bug is one of the insects that make it through winter as an adult.

passages.title: Follow the signs
passages.body: Some mammals keep moving through the woods all winter. Fishers are active through the cold months, and snow can preserve the tracks they leave as they travel.
passages.look_for: Follow a line of tracks from the side. See whether the prints fall in pairs and whether the spacing changes where the animal crossed roots or a log.

rows.name: Western Conifer Seed Bug
rows.interpretation: Adult Western Conifer Seed Bugs leave their feeding grounds on conifer cones in autumn and pass the winter under loose bark or in sheltered crevices, including in buildings.

sources.label: US Forest Service field guide to Western Conifer Seed Bug
Penn State Extension on Western Conifer Seed Bug life history

rows.name: American Mink
rows.interpretation: American mink hunt fish in winter and can surface through openings in stream ice. On snowy banks, their loping gait often leaves paired prints.

sources.label: New York State DEC on mink foraging and tracks

rows.name: Fisher
rows.interpretation: Fishers travel over snow in a bounding gait that often leaves prints in pairs. They mate in late winter and early spring, with young born around the same season the following year.

sources.label: New York State DEC on identifying Fisher signs

rows.name: Gray Fox
rows.interpretation: Gray foxes stay active on winter nights, hunting mice and rabbits. They can also climb trees by gripping the trunk with their front feet and pushing upward with their hind feet.

sources.label: US Forest Service on gray fox diet and winter activity
New York State DEC on gray fox climbing

bird_examples.name: Red Crossbill
bird_examples.note: This December checklist includes a photographed Red Crossbill at Kingfisher Hollow.
